## Proof

**Interpretation.** The hypothesis is: for every sequence $\{q_n\}$ with $q_n \to q$, the sequence $\{p_n\}$ gets arbitrarily close to $\{q_n\}$, i.e., for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $n$ such that $d(p_n, q_n) < \varepsilon$ (equivalently, $\inf_n d(p_n, q_n) = 0$). The question is whether this forces $p_n \to q$.

**Answer: No.** The implication fails. We give an explicit counterexample.

---

**Counterexample.** Take the metric space $(\mathbb{R}, |\cdot|)$ with $q = 0$. Define
$$
p_n = \begin{cases} 0 & n \text{ even}, \\ 1 & n \text{ odd}.\end{cases}
$$

**Claim 1 (Hypothesis holds).** Let $\{q_n\}$ be any sequence with $q_n \to 0$. Consider the subsequence at even indices: $p_{2k} = 0$ for all $k$, so
$$
d(p_{2k},\, q_{2k}) = |0 - q_{2k}| = |q_{2k}| \to 0 \quad (k \to \infty),
$$
since $q_n \to 0$ implies every subsequence $q_{2k} \to 0$. Therefore, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $k$ (hence $n = 2k$) with $d(p_n, q_n) < \varepsilon$. Thus $\inf_n d(p_n, q_n) = 0$ for every sequence $\{q_n\} \to 0$. ✓

**Claim 2 (Conclusion fails).** The subsequence $\{p_{2k+1}\}$ is constantly $1$, so
$$
d(p_{2k+1},\, 0) = 1 \quad \text{for all } k.
$$
Hence $p_n \not\to 0$: taking $\varepsilon = \tfrac{1}{2}$, for every $N$ there exists $n = 2k+1 \geq N$ with $d(p_n, 0) = 1 \geq \varepsilon$. ✗

---

**Why the implication breaks down.** The hypothesis only requires that $\{p_n\}$ *gets close to* $\{q_n\}$ at *some* index $n$. If $\{p_n\}$ has a subsequence already equal to (or converging to) $q$, then that subsequence alone satisfies the hypothesis for every $\{q_n\} \to q$—the behavior of the remaining terms is completely unconstrained. In the counterexample, the even-indexed subsequence $p_{2k} = 0 = q$ does all the work, while the odd-indexed subsequence stays at distance $1$ from $q$ forever.

**Remark.** If one strengthens the hypothesis to require $d(p_n, q_n) \to 0$ for *every* $\{q_n\} \to q$ (rather than just $\inf_n d(p_n,q_n)=0$), then the conclusion becomes trivially true: take the constant sequence $q_n = q$, which gives $d(p_n, q) \to 0$, i.e., $p_n \to q$. The interest—and the failure—lies in the weaker "arbitrarily close at some index" reading, under which the answer is **no**. $\blacksquare$

## Proof

**Interpretation.** The hypothesis is: for every sequence $\{q_n\}$ with $q_n \to q$, the sequence $\{p_n\}$ gets arbitrarily close to $\{q_n\}$, i.e., for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $n$ such that $d(p_n, q_n) < \varepsilon$ (equivalently, $\inf_n d(p_n, q_n) = 0$). The question is whether this forces $p_n \to q$.

**Answer: No.** The implication fails. We give an explicit counterexample.

---

**Counterexample.** Take the metric space $(\mathbb{R}, |\cdot|)$ with $q = 0$. Define
$$
p_n = \begin{cases} 0 & n \text{ even}, \\ 1 & n \text{ odd}.\end{cases}
$$

**Claim 1 (Hypothesis holds).** Let $\{q_n\}$ be any sequence with $q_n \to 0$. Consider the subsequence at even indices: $p_{2k} = 0$ for all $k$, so
$$
d(p_{2k},\, q_{2k}) = |0 - q_{2k}| = |q_{2k}| \to 0 \quad (k \to \infty),
$$
since $q_n \to 0$ implies every subsequence $q_{2k} \to 0$. Therefore, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $k$ (hence $n = 2k$) with $d(p_n, q_n) < \varepsilon$. Thus $\inf_n d(p_n, q_n) = 0$ for every sequence $\{q_n\} \to 0$. ✓

**Claim 2 (Conclusion fails).** The subsequence $\{p_{2k+1}\}$ is constantly $1$, so
$$
d(p_{2k+1},\, 0) = 1 \quad \text{for all } k.
$$
Hence $p_n \not\to 0$: taking $\varepsilon = \tfrac{1}{2}$, for every $N$ there exists $n = 2k+1 \geq N$ with $d(p_n, 0) = 1 \geq \varepsilon$. ✗

**Why the implication breaks down.** The hypothesis only requires that $\{p_n\}$ *gets close to* $\{q_n\}$ at *some* index $n$. If $\{p_n\}$ has a subsequence already equal to (or converging to) $q$, then that subsequence alone satisfies the hypothesis for every $\{q_n\} \to q$—the behavior of the remaining terms is completely unconstrained. In the counterexample, the even-indexed subsequence $p_{2k} = 0 = q$ does all the work, while the odd-indexed subsequence stays at distance $1$ from $q$ forever.

**Remark.** If one strengthens the hypothesis to require $d(p_n, q_n) \to 0$ for *every* $\{q_n\} \to q$ (rather than just $\inf_n d(p_n,q_n)=0$), then the conclusion becomes trivially true: take the constant sequence $q_n = q$, which gives $d(p_n, q) \to 0$, i.e., $p_n \to q$. The interest—and the failure—lies in the weaker "arbitrarily close at some index" reading, under which the answer is **no**. $\blacksquare$
